A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of miscellaneous bacterial agents of human diseases
A.q: Which vibrio causes gastroenteritis from raw seafood with symptoms similar to cholera?
opts: Vibrio vulnificus
Vibrio vulnificus is the raw-oyster vibrio that is dangerous in diabetes or liver disease; the cholera-like seafood gastroenteritis is Vibrio parahaemolyticus.
Vibrio parahaemolyticus
Correct: Vibrio parahaemolyticus causes gastroenteritis from raw seafood, with symptoms similar to cholera.
Vibrio cholerae El Tor
El Tor is a longer-surviving biotype of Vibrio cholerae itself; the cholera-like seafood vibrio is Vibrio parahaemolyticus.
Campylobacter fetus
Campylobacter fetus is an opportunist of debilitated persons and late pregnancy; the seafood vibrio is Vibrio parahaemolyticus.

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
A.q: Which organism most commonly causes gas gangrene?
opts: Clostridium tetani
Clostridium tetani causes tetanus, a neuromuscular disease, rather than gas gangrene.
Clostridium botulinum
Clostridium botulinum causes botulism, a paralytic intoxication, rather than gas gangrene.
Clostridium perfringens
Correct: Clostridium perfringens is the most common cause of myonecrosis (gas gangrene), though Clostridium novyi and Clostridium septicum can also cause it.
Clostridioides difficile
Clostridioides difficile causes antibiotic-associated colitis rather than gas gangrene.

A.io: 1 — Recall common infectious agents and the diseases that they cause
A.q: What can immunoelectrophoresis identify?
opts: The species of an unknown bacterium
Species identification comes from phenotypic, genotypic or serotyping approaches.
Specific antibody classes binding antigen in serum
Correct — IgG, IgM and the rest — and the technique is run on agarose or a similar gelling material.
The minimum inhibitory concentration of a drug
That is read from an MIC strip or inferred from disk diffusion.
Specific DNA sequences in a sample
Detecting specific DNA sequences in a sample is what the Southern blot does.

A.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire miscellaneous bacterial agents of human diseases
A.q: How is ornithosis transmitted to humans?
opts: From ticks
Ticks transmit Lyme disease and Rocky Mountain spotted fever; ornithosis comes from birds.
From birds
Correct: ornithosis (Chlamydophila psittaci) is a zoonosis transmitted to humans from birds and is highly communicable among all birds.
From cats
Cats transmit cat-scratch disease (Bartonella); ornithosis comes from birds.
From lice
Lice transmit epidemic typhus and trench fever; ornithosis comes from birds.

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
A.q: The raised yellow-white plaques shown line a patient's colon. Which organism produces them?
A.alt: Colonoscopy view of pink colon lining dotted with raised yellow-white plaques, two of them marked with arrows.
opts: Clostridium perfringens
Clostridium perfringens causes a mild, rapidly resolving gastroenteritis, not pseudomembranous colitis.
Listeria monocytogenes
Listeria is often mild in healthy adults and affects the brain and meninges in vulnerable patients rather than forming colonic plaques.
Bacillus cereus
Bacillus cereus causes a 24-hour toxin illness of vomiting or diarrhea without colonic plaques.
Clostridioides difficile
Correct: these are the pseudomembranes of antibiotic-associated colitis, sloughed necrotic intestinal lining.
A.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 47

A.io: 6 — Describe antimicrobial treatment strategies
A.q: What does MIC stand for?
opts: Maximum inhibitory concentration
It is the MINIMUM concentration that inhibits growth rather than a maximum.
Mean infectious count
The abbreviation refers to the inhibitory concentration of an antimicrobial agent.
Microbial identification code
It concerns antimicrobial susceptibility rather than identification.
Minimum inhibitory concentration
Correct, and MIC strips report it directly as a number rather than as the zone diameter the disk-diffusion method produces.

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, and methods of treatment, and prevention of cocci of medical importance
A.alt: Gram-stained smear of a freshly isolated organism, high magnification
A.q: A freshly isolated organism is Gram stained as shown: purple, Gram-positive spheres lie in long, winding chains. Which genus fits this arrangement?
opts: Streptococcus
Correct: Gram-positive spherical or ovoid cocci arranged in long chains are the streptococci.
Staphylococcus
Staphylococci are Gram-positive cocci too, but they are arranged in irregular clusters rather than long chains.
Neisseria
Neisseria are Gram-negative, bean-shaped diplococci, pairs rather than the Gram-positive chains seen here.
Moraxella
Moraxella are Gram-negative diplococci on mucous membranes, pairs rather than the Gram-positive chains seen here.
A.cite: PAJ5200.Cocci of Med importance.pptx, Slides 3, 21, 56, 78 and image on Slide 22

A.io: 6 — Define reportable disease
A.q: What does collecting reportable disease data allow authorities to do?
opts: Monitor disease, warn of outbreaks
Correct: data collection lets authorities monitor the disease and provides early warning of potential outbreaks.
Prove what causes each disease
Reports monitor disease and warn of outbreaks; epidemiology infers causation from association and other factors, and does not prove the cause of each disease.
Bill patients for public testing
Billing is not the purpose; reportable disease data let authorities monitor disease and get early warning of outbreaks.
Replace physicians' diagnoses
Reports depend on diagnoses rather than replacing them; their purpose is monitoring and early warning of outbreaks.
A.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 21 and 43

A.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
A.q: What are exposures associated with a difference in disease risk often called?
opts: Indicators
An indicator is a measurable factor estimating the size of a health problem; exposures linked to disease risk are risk factors.
Risk factors
Correct: exposures associated with a difference in disease risk are often called risk factors.
Vehicles
A vehicle is an environmental mode of communication bringing host and agent together; exposures linked to risk are risk factors.
Confounders
A confounded association is one level of the pyramid of associations; exposures associated with disease risk are called risk factors.

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, and methods of treatment, and prevention of cocci of medical importance
A.q: After a positive catalase test, which test separates Staphylococcus aureus from the other staphylococci?
opts: Bacitracin disc
Bacitracin sensitivity is used among beta-hemolytic streptococci, to pick out group A.
Coagulase test
Correct: Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase positive, while the other staphylococci are coagulase negative.
Optochin disc
Optochin sensitivity is used among alpha-hemolytic streptococci, to pick out Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Bile esculin test
Bile esculin hydrolysis is a phenotypic culture test listed for the streptococci.

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, and methods of treatment, and prevention of cocci of medical importance
A.q: Which gonococcal surface structures aid attachment and slow phagocytosis?
opts: Flagella
Neisseria develop no flagella and are non-motile; fimbriae give the gonococcus attachment.
Fimbriae
Correct: fimbriae and other surface molecules give attachment and slow phagocytosis.
Endospores
Neisseria are non-spore-forming; fimbriae and other surface molecules give attachment and slow phagocytosis.
M-protein
M-protein is the Streptococcus pyogenes antigen that resists phagocytosis.

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
A.q: Which problem is the main force driving the search for novel antimicrobial therapies?
opts: Shortages of antibiotic raw materials
Supply shortages are not what drives the search; the driver is microbes becoming resistant, fed by overuse and inappropriate prescribing.
Antibiotics that cost too much
Price is not the stated driver; antibiotics are losing effectiveness because microbes become resistant to them.
Antimicrobial resistance

Correct: resistance to antimicrobials and antibiotics heads the list of what drives the need for novel therapies, fed by overuse in agriculture, inappropriate prescribing and patients not finishing treatment.
Viruses replacing bacteria as pathogens
Bacteria remain major pathogens; the problem is that more of them resist the antibiotics we have, which is why alternatives are sought.

A.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire cocci of medical importance
A.q: In females, staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome is classically associated with what?
opts: Contaminated dessert
Food contaminated with heat-stable enterotoxin causes staphylococcal food intoxication rather than toxic shock.
A dental procedure
Dental procedures let viridans streptococci into the blood; they are not the classic source of toxic shock.
Shared bath towels
Shared towels spread staphylococcal skin infection; the classic association of toxic shock in females is tampon use.
Improper tampon use
Correct: toxic shock syndrome in females classically originates from improper tampon use, a toxemia leading to shock and organ failure.

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, and methods of treatment, and prevention of cocci of medical importance
A.alt: Close view of skin lesions around a mouth
A.q: Which streptococcal skin infection produces lesions like these around the mouth, superficial lesions that have broken and formed thick crusts?
opts: Erysipelas
Erysipelas enters through a break in the skin and spreads to the dermis and subcutaneous tissues rather than forming broken, crusted superficial lesions.
Carbuncle
A carbuncle is a larger, deeper staphylococcal lesion, a cluster of interconnected furuncles, not a streptococcal crust.
Impetigo
Correct: impetigo (pyoderma) is superficial lesions that break and form a highly contagious crust.
Scarlet fever
Scarlet fever is a systemic infection with fever and a red rash from erythrogenic toxin, not crusted lesions around the mouth.

A.io: 9 — Compare and contrast immunotherapy strategies
A.q: What is the main challenge of oncolytic viral therapy?
opts: The virus destroys normal cells
Damage to normal cells is not the main challenge: the virus attacks them but has little effect, infecting them without replicating, so they stay undamaged.
The virus cannot infect tumor cells
The virus does infect and replicate in tumor cells, lysing them and releasing progeny.
No virus is naturally oncolytic
Some viruses are naturally oncolytic, such as mumps, while others are engineered.
Immunity may clear the virus first
Correct. The immune system may wipe out the oncolytic virus before it does its job, and only a few are approved, just one in the United States, for melanoma.
A.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 80 (text and image)

A.io: 1 — Recall common infectious agents and the diseases that they cause
A.q: What instrument does the polymerase chain reaction use?
opts: A thermal cycler
Correct, to amplify specific bits of DNA or RNA. The basic concept was invented by Kary Mullis and colleagues.
An electrophoresis tank
Electrophoresis separates the products; the amplification itself uses a thermal cycler.
A 96-well plate reader
Those plates are used in enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays.
A fluorescence microscope
A fluorescence microscope is used in fluorescent antibody testing rather than for amplification.

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, and methods of treatment, and prevention of cocci of medical importance
A.q: What does a candle jar provide when culturing pathogenic Neisseria on chocolate agar?
opts: Extra salt in the medium
Salt selection is the job of mannitol salts agar, which suits staphylococci rather than Neisseria.
Complete absence of air
A candle jar enriches carbon dioxide; Neisseria are aerobic or microaerophilic, not strict anaerobes.
Enhanced carbon dioxide
Correct: pathogenic species need carbon dioxide-enhanced chambers, such as chocolate agar in a candle jar.
Red cells for hemolysis
Reading hemolysis is the job of blood agar; the candle jar supplies the carbon dioxide.

A.io: 1 — Recall common infectious agents and the diseases that they cause
A.q: Why does faster diagnosis matter to the patient?
opts: Proper treatment can begin in a timely manner
Correct, and precise automated methods deliver quick results — which is the clinical argument for genotypic testing over waiting for growth.
It reduces the cost of the laboratory test
The stated advantage is timeliness of treatment rather than cost.
It removes the need for sensitivity testing
Susceptibility still has to be determined, whether by disk diffusion or another method.
It guarantees the organism is the cause of disease
Whether the organism recovered is causing the disease remains a separate question.

A.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology
A.q: In the host-agent-environment triad, which of these is a host factor?
opts: Immunologic status
Correct: host factors are genetic endowment, immunologic status, personal characteristics, personal behavior, and definitive versus intermediate host in vector-borne disease.
Crowded housing
Living conditions such as crowding belong to the environment, not the host.
A biting vector
A vector is one of the environment's modes of communication that bring host and agent together.
A dietary allergen
Allergens are listed among the agents (environmental agents); immunologic status is a host factor.
A.cite: Lecture 12 Dr. Webster - Epidemiology.pptx, Slide 38, 39 and 40

A.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
A.q: What is herd immunity?
opts: Resistance one person inherits from parents
Inherited resistance is one route to an individual's immunity; herd immunity is the number or percentage of immune persons in a population.
A vaccine given to every member of a herd
Vaccination contributes to herd immunity but is not its definition; herd immunity is the number or share of immune persons in a population.
Antibody made after a single infection
Antibody after infection is one person's acquired resistance; herd immunity measures how many in the population are immune.
The share of a population that is immune
Correct: herd immunity is the cumulative number of immune persons in a population, or the percentage of the population that is immune.

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
A.q: Which findings support a diagnosis of leprosy?
opts: Numb skin with acid-fast bacilli
Correct: numbness, loss of heat and cold sensitivity, thickened earlobes and a chronic stuffy nose, with acid-fast bacilli in lesions or nasal discharge.
A pseudomembrane and myocarditis
A pseudomembrane with myocarditis is respiratory diphtheria with toxemia.
Watery diarrhea after antibiotics
Diarrhea after antibiotics points to Clostridioides difficile.
A painless papule turning black
A painless papule becoming a black eschar is cutaneous anthrax.
A.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 87

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of miscellaneous bacterial agents of human diseases
A.q: Which description fits Campylobacter?
opts: Comma-shaped single rods
Comma-shaped rods are Vibrio; Campylobacter is curved or spiral, often in S-shaped or gull-winged pairs.
Tight coils with hooked ends
Tight coils with hooked ends are Leptospira, a spirochete; Campylobacter forms curved rods in gull-winged pairs.
Curved rods in gull-winged pairs
Correct: campylobacters are Gram-negative slender, curved or spiral rods, often S-shaped or gull-winged pairs, with a single polar flagellum.
Wall-less, highly variable cells
Lacking a wall and highly pleomorphic describes Mycoplasma; Campylobacter is a curved rod in gull-winged pairs.

A.io: 5 — Explain the immunology of transplantations and tissue histocompatibility
A.q: A patient receives a heart valve taken from a pig. Which graft type is this?
opts: A xenograft
Correct. A xenograft is tissue from another species, here a pig transplanted into a human.
An allograft
An allograft comes from another member of the SAME species; a pig valve in a human crosses species.
An isograft
An isograft comes from a genetically identical twin, which a pig donor clearly is not.
An autograft
An autograft is the patient's own tissue moved to a new site, such as a vein graft from the leg.
A.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 43

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
A.q: Which spore positions distinguish Bacillus anthracis from Clostridium tetani?
opts: Terminal in Bacillus anthracis, central in Clostridium tetani
This reverses the pair: the Bacillus anthracis spore is central and the Clostridium tetani spore sits at one end of the rod.
Central in Bacillus anthracis, terminal in Clostridium tetani
Correct: Bacillus anthracis has central spores, while the spore of Clostridium tetani sits at one end of the rod, a terminal spore that swells it.
Central in both, but larger in Clostridium tetani
The two differ in position, not just size: the Bacillus anthracis spore is central and the Clostridium tetani spore is terminal.
Terminal in both Bacillus anthracis and Clostridium tetani
The Clostridium tetani spore is terminal, but the Bacillus anthracis spore is central, in the middle of the cell.
A.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 8 and image on Slide 28

A.io: 2 — Describe fecal microbiota transplant (FMT)
A.q: Donor screening for fecal microbiota transplant is modeled on which other kind of screening?
opts: Organ transplant tissue typing
Tissue typing matches immune antigens; stool donor screening is modeled on blood bank screening for pathogens.
Blood bank donor screening
Correct: stool donor screening is similar to blood bank screening, to reduce the risk from blood-borne and other pathogens.
Newborn genetic screening
Genetic screening is unrelated; stool donor screening resembles blood bank screening for pathogens.
Cancer screening by colonoscopy
Colonoscopy may deliver the transplant, but donor screening is modeled on blood bank screening.

A.io: 1 — Recall common infectious agents and the diseases that they cause
A.q: What does the extreme specificity of antibodies let serological methods do?
opts: Detect only large amounts
These methods are very sensitive and detect small amounts; specificity concerns which antigen an antibody binds, not how much is present.
Amplify the signal enzymatically
An enzyme producing a colored product is how the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay reads out; it is not what antibody specificity gives serology.
Identify an unknown microbe
Correct: in serotyping, an unknown microbe is mixed with antibodies of known specificity, and a reaction shows a match between antibody and antigen that identifies the microbe.
Run in duplicate every time
Running tests in duplicate is not what specificity provides; specificity means an antibody binds its own antigen, so known antibodies can identify a microbe.
A.cite: PAJ5200.Diagnosing Infections-2.pptx, Slides 30, 32, 50 and image on Slide 31

A.io: 8 — Explain the mechanisms of carcinogenesis
A.q: Some tumor cells cleave a stress molecule that natural killer cells recognize and release it in soluble form. What is the effect?
opts: Natural killer cells destroy it faster
Normally surface stress molecules mark the cell for killing; shedding them in soluble form blocks that recognition.
Complement lyses the tumor cell
The mechanism shown involves lymphocyte receptors, not complement lysis.
The tumor cell escapes being killed
Correct. The soluble molecule binds the killing receptor on natural killer and gamma-delta T cells, so the variant tumor cell is not killed and proliferates.
Mast cells degranulate at the tumor
Mast cell degranulation is the effector step of type I allergy, not of tumor evasion.
A.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 71

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
A.q: Who is most at risk of severe listeriosis?
opts: Fetuses, neonates, the immunocompromised
Correct: in these groups it affects the brain and meninges and causes fetal loss and newborn deaths, while healthy adults usually have mild illness.
Healthy young adults after a large meal
In healthy adults listeriosis is often mild or subclinical, with fever, diarrhea and sore throat.
Farmers who handle livestock daily
Pig handlers are at risk of Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae; severe listeriosis strikes the immunocompromised, fetuses and neonates.
Metal workers who inhale welding fumes
Welders are the group affected by welder's anthrax, caused by Bacillus cereus.
A.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 55

A.io: 1 — Recall common infectious agents and the diseases that they cause
A.q: What kind of technique are the color-changing rapid strep tests?
opts: A precipitation reaction in gel
Precipitation requires a gel or liquid matrix and is slower and less sensitive than agglutination.
An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
The ELISA uses an enzyme-antibody complex producing a chromogen in a well plate.
A modified agglutination technique
Correct, which places them with blood typing and the latex pregnancy test rather than with the precipitation methods.
A genotypic amplification method
Genotypic methods assess the organism's nucleic acid rather than using antibody.

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
A.q: Penicillin, vancomycin and azithromycin share which pattern?
opts: Resistance appeared before each drug was discovered
Resistance was detected after each drug came into widespread clinical use, not before it was discovered.
Resistance has never been detected to any of them
Resistance has been detected to all three: penicillin, vancomycin and azithromycin each met resistant bacteria after coming into wide use.
Resistance took about a century to appear
It took years, not a century; each drug met resistance within a few years to about two decades of widespread use.
Resistance appeared within years of widespread use
Correct: for each drug, resistance was first detected within a few years to about two decades of its widespread clinical use, a reminder that use selects for resistance.

A.io: 1 — Recall common infectious agents and the diseases that they cause
A.q: Why do viruses present special difficulties for diagnosis?
opts: They cannot be detected by any immunological method
Rapid point of care tests based on antigen-antibody reactions are specifically used for viruses.
They grow too quickly to be captured
The difficulty is that they require a specific host cell type, making culture labor intensive.
They have no nucleic acid to sequence
Viruses carry nucleic acid, and genotypic methods can be applied to them.
They are not cells, and need a host cell
Correct, which makes them labor intensive to culture — and is why rapid point of care tests based on antigen-antibody reactions matter so much here. The host cell must be a specific type.

A.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
A.q: Which blood test result supports an allergy diagnosis?
opts: Raised IgG against the allergen
Allergen-specific IgG is what desensitization therapy aims to raise, blocking the allergen from IgE; the allergy blood test looks for specific IgE.
Complement consumption
Complement activation features in type II and type III hypersensitivity; the blood test that supports an allergy looks for specific IgE.
Specific IgE to the allergen
Correct: blood tests for allergy look for specific IgE to the suspected allergen and for increased basophils; skin testing with wheal and flare reactions is the other route.
Positive blood culture
A positive blood culture points to infection, which allergy testing aims to tell apart; the allergy blood test looks for specific IgE.
A.cite: Lecture 7  Dr. Webster  Disorders in Immunity.pptx, Slide 25, 29, 32 and 38

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
A.q: Which patients most commonly receive empiric antibiotic therapy?
opts: Healthy patients with no symptoms
Treating people without symptoms would be prophylaxis or overuse; empiric therapy is for sick patients, especially critically ill ones.
Critically ill or emergent patients
Correct: empiric therapy is common in human and veterinary medicine, especially for critically ill or emergent patients who cannot wait for results.
Patients whose cultures are already back
Once cultures are back, therapy is directed by the results; empiric therapy is given before they are available.
Only patients with viral infections
Antibiotics do not treat viruses; empiric therapy covers a suspected bacterial infection in a sick patient before results return.

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
A.q: What is the current name of Propionibacterium acnes?
opts: Corynebacterium acnes
Corynebacterium is a separate irregular genus, home of Corynebacterium diphtheriae; the new name is Cutibacterium acnes.
Clostridioides acnes
Clostridioides is the new genus for the spore-forming difficile organism; the acne organism is Cutibacterium acnes.
Cutibacterium acnes
Correct: the genus Propionibacterium has been reclassified as Cutibacterium, so the acne organism is Cutibacterium acnes.
Actinomyces acnes
Actinomyces is a filamentous genus; Propionibacterium acnes is now Cutibacterium acnes.
A.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 65

A.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
A.q: Foodborne botulism is most associated with which foods?
opts: Cooked rice left out and reheated
Reheated rice is the classic vehicle of Bacillus cereus food poisoning.
Unpasteurized soft cheeses
Soft cheeses and dairy are the vehicles of Listeria monocytogenes.
Low-acid, home-canned vegetables
Correct: home-canned green beans and corn are the classic sources, though meats, fish and dairy can also carry it.
Undercooked ground chicken
Undercooked meat and poultry are linked to listeriosis and Clostridium perfringens rather than to botulism.
A.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 34

A.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
A.q: Why is pulmonary anthrax called woolsorters' disease?
opts: Wool fibers cut the skin and let spores in
Spores entering through cuts cause cutaneous anthrax; woolsorters' disease is the inhaled, pulmonary form.
Sorters swallow spores from their hands
Swallowed spores in meat cause gastrointestinal anthrax; woolsorters' disease is acquired by inhalation.
Sheep transmit the bacillus by biting
Anthrax is a zoonosis acquired from spores, not by animal bites; woolsorters inhale spores from the wool.
Sorters inhale spores from infected wool
Correct: it is acquired by inhaling spores from infected animal products or soil, so people handling wool from infected sheep were exposed.
A.cite: Lecture 9 Dr. Webster Gram positive Bacilli.pptx, Slide 13

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of miscellaneous bacterial agents of human diseases
A.q: Which set of findings fits acute leptospirosis?
opts: Fever, aches, conjunctivitis
Correct: leptospirosis brings a sudden high fever, chills, headache, muscle aches, conjunctivitis and vomiting; long-term infection may affect the kidneys and liver.
Fever, sore throat, palm rash
Fever, sore throat and a palm and sole rash are secondary syphilis; leptospirosis gives sudden fever, muscle aches and conjunctivitis.
Rice water stool, dehydration
Rice water stool and dehydration are cholera; leptospirosis gives sudden high fever, muscle aches and conjunctivitis.
Fever, chest pain, sore throat
Fever, chest pain and sore throat are Mycoplasma pneumoniae's primary atypical pneumonia; leptospirosis adds conjunctivitis to fever and aches.

A.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
A.q: Which regulatory hurdle does phage therapy face in the United States?
opts: No phage product is yet approved as a medicine

Correct: bacterial viruses are not yet established as approved medicinal products, so regulatory clearance is a concern; investigational drug status and emergency use authorization are routes around it.
Phages are classed as controlled substances
They are not controlled substances; the hurdle is that no phage product is yet approved as a medicine.
Phages are already fully approved for all infections
No phage product has been approved as a medicine for routine use; clearance still needs special routes.
Phages may be sold only as dietary supplements
Phages are not sold as supplements for therapy; the hurdle is that no phage product is yet approved as a medicine.

A.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, and methods of treatment, and prevention of cocci of medical importance
A.q: Which staphylococcus infrequently lives on skin, intestine and vagina and may cause urinary tract infection?
opts: Staphylococcus capitis
Staphylococcus capitis lives on the scalp, face and external ear.
Staphylococcus hominis
Staphylococcus hominis lives around the apocrine sweat glands of the armpits and groin.
Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase positive and is carried mostly in the anterior nares.
Staphylococcus saprophyticus
Correct: Staphylococcus saprophyticus infrequently lives on skin, intestine and vagina and may cause urinary tract infection.

A.io: 4 — Describe other alternative therapies to antibiotic use
A.q: According to one hypothesis about cooking spices, where should spice use be heaviest?
opts: In hot climates where food spoils quickly
Correct: the hypothesis is that spice use is heaviest where a hot climate goes with rapid food spoilage, because some herbs and spices kill bacteria and fungi.
In cold climates with long winters
The prediction is the reverse: hot climates with rapid food spoilage, where antimicrobial spices would help most.
Wherever refrigeration is most common
Refrigeration slows spoilage and would lessen the need; the hypothesis points to hot climates with rapid spoilage.
Only in coastal fishing regions
Coastline is not the variable; the hypothesis ties heavy spice use to hot climates and fast food spoilage.

A.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire cocci of medical importance
A.q: A 26-year-old soldier evacuated from Afghanistan develops a multidrug-resistant infection with coccobacilli in a military hospital. Which organism is most likely?
opts: Acinetobacter baumannii
Correct: these multidrug-resistant coccobacilli are becoming an important hospital-acquired infection, especially in military hospitals.
Moraxella catarrhalis
Moraxella catarrhalis is a nasopharyngeal diplococcus, an opportunist in cancer, diabetic and alcoholic patients.
Neisseria meningitidis
Neisseria meningitidis is a diplococcus spread from the nasopharynx in close quarters, not a multidrug-resistant coccobacillus.
Enterococcus faecalis
Enterococcus faecalis is a Gram-positive coccus of the large intestine rather than a Gram-negative coccobacillus.

A.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
A.q: What does the hygiene hypothesis propose?
opts: Underused immune systems are less successfully regulated

Correct. Where worms were removed by better sanitation and treatment, as in Western Europe and North America, the idea is that this arm of the immune system is underused and less well regulated, so it may overreact to harmless things.
Exposure to allergens in childhood causes lifelong allergy
The hypothesis runs the opposite way, attributing allergy to too LITTLE early immune challenge.
Hygiene practices directly damage epithelial barriers
The proposed mechanism concerns regulation of the immune system rather than barrier damage.

Any phage that infects human cells
Phages do not infect human cells, and therapy needs lytic phages that kill the target bacterium.
A lytic phage
Correct: therapy needs lytic phages, which replicate and burst the bacterium; lysogenic phages instead fold their genome into the host.
A phage with no genome
A phage with no genome could not replicate; therapy needs lytic phages.

Treatment of a resistant superbug
No infection is present; the drug prevents infection in an immunocompromised patient, which is prophylaxis.
Desensitization to the transplanted organ

Correct: antimicrobial prophylaxis is used in immunocompromised patients, such as those with human immunodeficiency virus infection, cancer chemotherapy or transplant immunosuppression.

Monitoring the genetic makeup of pathogens
Correct: genomic epidemiology is the process of monitoring the genetic makeup of the pathogens that cause disease, made possible by advances in sequencing.
Testing new vaccines in clinical trials

Mapping cases by home and workplace
Mapping where cases lived and worked is a spot map, descriptive epidemiology; genomic epidemiology monitors pathogens' genetic makeup.

Crude mortality

Prevalence
Correct: all cases present at or during a time period, over the population, is prevalence; a survey of who currently has a condition measures it.
Attack rate

A peptic ulcer

Erythema migrans
Erythema migrans is the expanding bull's-eye rash at a tick bite in Lyme disease, not a raised late syphilitic lesion.
A cat-scratch papule
Cat-scratch disease follows a clawing injury by a cat and is caused by Bartonella; a late lesion of syphilis is a gumma.
A gumma
Correct: gummas develop in tertiary syphilis, the late stage that can last 20 years or longer, along with neurological and cardiovascular symptoms.

Host-membrane lipids
Special lipids from host membranes are what Mycoplasma requires; rickettsias require live host cells.
A salt-rich medium
Salt tolerance belongs to the seafood vibrios; rickettsias need live cells to be cultivated.
Live host cells
Correct: rickettsias are very small intracellular parasites that require live cells for cultivation.

Urinary, wound and skin

Pharyngitis and scarlet fever belong to group A Streptococcus pyogenes.
Caries and periodontitis
Dental caries, gingivitis and periodontitis are linked to the viridans streptococci.

Immune complex deposition in the alveolar membrane

Complement-mediated lysis of airway epithelium
Complement lysis of epithelium characterizes type II rather than the acute asthmatic response.
Bronchial smooth muscle contraction with increased mucus

Corynebacterium diphtheriae

Actinomyces israelii

All four types
Type I is excluded; autoimmune disease uses types II, III and IV.
Type IV only
Type IV is one of three involved; types II and III also cause autoimmune disease.
All except type I
Correct. Autoimmunity involves types II, III and IV, but not type I, the immunoglobulin E mediated allergy.

Robert Koch

John Snow
Correct: John Snow, an anesthesiologist, used epidemiologic approaches to understand the London cholera epidemic and is called the father of field epidemiology.
John Graunt
John Graunt pioneered tabulating mortality as rates and ratios; field epidemiology traces to John Snow's cholera investigations.

It has a single polar flagellum

Viral causes such as the human immunodeficiency virus produce SECONDARY immunodeficiency.

Genomic methods identify pathogens by their genetic makeup, the opposite of a clinical-feature definition; this is syndromic surveillance.
Syndromic surveillance

There are no MHC molecules on red blood cells
Correct, so ABO is the critical matching system. You carry antibodies in your serum against the antigens you lack, and mismatch can be fatal through complement activation and lysis.

They do not; the absence of MHC on red cells is the stated reason ABO matters.
Transfused cells are permanent replacements
Transfusions are described as temporary rather than as permanent cell replacements.

Plaque sits on the enamel surface; it damages enamel through the acid its bacteria produce.
Its bacteria make acid

Scarlet fever

Rheumatic fever

Disease prioritization

Public health surveillance

Congenital agammaglobulinemia
Congenital agammaglobulinemia is a PRIMARY B cell immunodeficiency.
Suppression after chemotherapy

Severe combined immunodeficiency
Severe combined immunodeficiency is congenital, a PRIMARY defect of both lymphocyte limbs.

Gummas

Palm and sole rashes

Hutchinson's teeth

Its specific soluble substance

Testing serum in the laboratory is serology, which is in vitro.

No culture is involved; antigen is introduced into the patient.
It measures antibody titre in binding antibody units
Antibody titre in binding antibody units is reported by in vitro serological testing rather than in vivo.
Antigen is introduced directly into the body
Correct, to determine the presence or absence of antibodies. The tuberculin skin test and allergy testing are the named examples.

Catalase positive
Catalase positivity is the staphylococcal result, the bubbling with hydrogen peroxide that separates the two genera.
Coagulase positive

Oxidase positive

B.q: Where are the nonsyphilitic treponematoses endemic?

Arid regions and the Global South

The northeastern United States

Worldwide, wherever lice are

B.q: What is the main purpose of fecal microbiota transplant?

Delivering a high-dose antibiotic

Vaccinating against intestinal viruses

Giardia and Cryptosporidium

None; parasites are not screened
Parasites are screened: Giardia and Cryptosporidium are on the list.

B.io: 1 — Distinguish between descriptive and analytic epidemiology

Estimate measures of association
Estimating associations comes after the population is defined, measures created and a sample taken.
Assess external validity
Assessing whether results apply to other populations is the last step; the first is defining the population of interest.

Eliminating tuberculosis

Eradicating smallpox

Ending influenza outbreaks

Specific DNA sequences

About 90%

B.io: 1 — Recall common infectious agents and the diseases that they cause
B.q: What limits the usefulness of a rapid immunological test?
opts: It cannot detect antigen, only antibody
Specific antibodies are used to DETECT antigens in these methods.
You need a hypothesis to target it
Correct — fever, sore throat and pus-pockets on the tonsils lead you to suspect strep throat, and only then does the rapid test answer the question.
It always requires culture first
Immunological methods may or may not require culturing, so culture is not a precondition.
It takes longer than culture
The rapid strep test takes ten to fifteen minutes, far less than culture.

B.io: 3 — Describe phage therapy
B.q: By which two life cycles can bacteriophages replicate?
opts: Lytic and lysogenic
Correct: phages replicate by a lytic cycle, which bursts the host bacterium, or a lysogenic cycle, which folds the phage genome into the host.
Binary fission and budding
Binary fission and budding are how bacteria and yeasts reproduce; phages use lytic or lysogenic cycles.
Sporulation and germination
Sporulation is how some bacteria survive harsh conditions; phages replicate by lytic or lysogenic cycles.
Conjugation and transformation
Conjugation and transformation are ways bacteria exchange DNA; phages replicate by lytic or lysogenic cycles.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
B.q: Why do so few wounds carrying Clostridium perfringens develop myonecrosis?
opts: Most wounds carry strains that lack spores
The organism forms spores readily; disease depends on host factors, dead tissue and low oxygen.
Vaccination protects most of the population
No vaccine against myonecrosis is available; disease depends on dead tissue and anaerobic conditions.
It needs dead tissue and low oxygen
Correct: it is not highly invasive, so although most contaminated wounds carry it, disease needs damaged, dead tissue and anaerobic conditions.
It is killed rapidly by skin bacteria
Other bacteria help rather than hinder it, by using up oxygen in a mixed infection.

B.io: 4 — Identify common sources of epidemiologic data
B.q: Air-quality ratings collected by sensors are which source of epidemiologic data?
opts: Individual persons
Individual persons are surveyed or given questionnaires; sensor readings of air quality are environmental data.
The environment
Correct: the environment supplies data through samples and sensors for environmental changes, including air-quality ratings.
Health care providers
Providers notify the health department of cases of certain diseases; air-quality ratings come from the environment.
Nonhealth-related sources
Nonhealth-related sources are financial and legal records; air-quality sensor data are environmental.

B.io: 1 — Recall common infectious agents and the diseases that they cause
B.q: Which category of method usually does NOT require culturing?
opts: Phenotypic
Phenotypic methods may require longer to reach a diagnosis precisely because the microbes must be cultured first.
Immunological
Immunological methods may or may not require culturing, so they are not the category defined by avoiding it.
All three require culture
Genotypic methods usually do not, and immunological ones may not either.
Genotypic
Correct, which is the whole practical point of it — slow growers such as Mycobacterium and difficult ones such as Legionella can be identified without waiting for growth.

B.io: 6 — Describe etiology autoimmune conditions
B.q: Which predisposition to autoimmune conditions is described?
opts: Men are affected more than women
It is the reverse: women are more likely than men to have autoimmune conditions.
Women are affected more than men
Correct. Women are more likely to have autoimmune conditions than men, and autoimmunities also run in families.
They do not run in families
Autoimmunities DO run in families; there are genetic as well as gender predispositions.
They affect only one organ each
Disruption of function can be systemic OR organ specific, so a single-organ rule is wrong.

B.q: Which condition produces the facial lesions shown, deep, thick nodules that badly disfigure the nose, brow and lips?
B.alt: Close view of a man's face with skin lesions.
opts: Tuberculoid leprosy
Tuberculoid leprosy gives shallow, asymmetrical lesions with local loss of pain sensation, not deep nodules.
Cutaneous anthrax
Cutaneous anthrax produces a single black necrotic eschar after a painless papule, not many nodules across the face.
Cervicofacial actinomycosis
Cervicofacial actinomycosis is a complication of an oral infection, a chronic infection of deeper tissue, not deep nodules across the whole face.
Lepromatous leprosy
Correct: a deeply nodular infection that severely disfigures the face is lepromatous leprosy, the widely disseminated form.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, and methods of treatment, and prevention of cocci of medical importance
B.q: How is gonococcal conjunctivitis of the newborn prevented?
opts: Topical antibiotics at birth
Correct: it is prevented by topical antibiotic prophylaxis immediately after birth.
Routine cesarean delivery
Cesarean delivery is not the preventive measure for gonorrhea; topical antibiotic prophylaxis at birth is.
A conjugate vaccine at birth
The conjugate vaccine is pneumococcal, for children 2 to 23 months; no gonococcal vaccine is listed.
Long-term oral penicillin
Long-term penicillin prophylaxis is for people with a history of rheumatic fever.

B.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
B.q: What are the systemic targets of a type I reaction?
opts: Skin, conjunctiva and nasal mucosa
Those are among the GENERAL targets rather than the systemic ones.
Red blood cells and platelets
Those are targets in type II reactions such as transfusion incompatibility.
Smooth muscle, mucous glands, nerve
Correct, and the responses are vascular dilation and constriction, producing changes in blood pressure and respiration.
Basement membranes of epithelial tissue
Basement membranes of epithelial tissue are where type III immune complexes deposit instead.

B.io: 1 — Recall common infectious agents and the diseases that they cause
B.q: What is serology?
opts: In vitro diagnostic testing of serum samples
Correct, and because antibodies are extremely specific for their antigens, these methods can tell close relatives apart; they are also very sensitive, able to detect small amounts.
In vivo introduction of antigen into the body
That describes in vivo testing such as the tuberculin skin test and allergy testing.
Culture of an organism on selective media
Culturing an organism on selective media is a phenotypic approach requiring growth rather than serology.
Amplification of nucleic acid from a specimen
Amplifying nucleic acid from a specimen is the polymerase chain reaction, a genotypic method.

B.io: 1 — Recall common infectious agents and the diseases that they cause
B.q: What do universal precautions achieve?
opts: They eliminate the risk of transmission entirely
They are specifically described as mitigating rather than eliminating the risk.
They sterilize the specimen before handling
Universal precautions protect the handler rather than sterilizing or treating the specimen itself.
They mitigate but do not eliminate transmission risk
Correct, which is why they are paired with aseptic procedure rather than relied on alone. Gloves and face shields or masks are the named examples.
They are needed only for known infectious specimens
All specimens are treated as potentially infectious, so the precautions are not applied selectively.

B.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire miscellaneous bacterial agents of human diseases
B.q: Which animals are the reservoirs of Borrelia hermsii?
opts: Squirrels and chipmunks
Correct: the mammalian reservoirs of Borrelia hermsii, the cause of relapsing fever, are squirrels, chipmunks and wild rodents, and it is spread by ticks.
Domestic cats
Cats are linked to cat-scratch disease from Bartonella; relapsing fever's reservoirs are squirrels, chipmunks and wild rodents.
Cattle and sheep
Cattle, sheep and goats pass Campylobacter fetus between themselves; relapsing fever's reservoirs are squirrels, chipmunks and wild rodents.
Pet birds
Birds transmit Chlamydophila psittaci, the cause of ornithosis; relapsing fever's reservoirs are squirrels, chipmunks and wild rodents.

B.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
B.q: An infection spreads from person to person through a community. Which type of epidemic is this?
opts: Common source, point
A point source exposes a group to one source over a short time; person-to-person spread is propagated.
Common source, continuous
A continuous common source exposes people to the same source over a longer time; person-to-person spread is propagated.
Propagated
Correct: a propagated epidemic is person-to-person transmission, reflecting spreading infection that may be extended.
Endemic
Endemic describes chronically low levels, not a type of epidemic; person-to-person spread is a propagated epidemic.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, and methods of treatment, and prevention of cocci of medical importance
B.q: A pregnant woman is expected to deliver vaginally. What is recommended for group B Streptococcus?
opts: Vaccinate the infant at birth
No group B vaccine is listed; protection comes from screening the mother and treating during delivery.
Screen her and treat if positive
Correct: pregnant women should be screened and treated, usually with intravenous antibiotics during vaginal delivery.
Plan a routine cesarean
Cesarean delivery is not the listed measure; the mother is screened and, if positive, treated during vaginal delivery.
Give lifelong penicillin
Long-term penicillin prophylaxis is for people with a history of rheumatic fever or recurrent strep throat.

B.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
B.q: A county counts residents newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes during the past year and divides by the county's residents at midyear. What is it measuring?
opts: Prevalence
Prevalence would count all residents who have diabetes, new and old; counting only the newly diagnosed measures incidence.
Cause-specific mortality
Cause-specific mortality counts deaths from a specific cause; this counts new diagnoses, which is incidence.
Incidence
Correct: new cases arising during a given period, over the population, is incidence; the numerator of incidence is new cases only.
Case fatality rate
The case fatality rate is deaths over total cases; new diagnoses over the population is incidence.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of miscellaneous bacterial agents of human diseases
B.q: Why can Vibrio cholerae need a very large infectious dose?
opts: It must first enter the blood
Vibrio cholerae never needs the blood; it is noninvasive and acts in the small intestine once it has passed the stomach.
It must first multiply in urine
Shedding in urine is how Leptospira spreads; the cholera dose is high because the vibrios must pass through the stomach.
It must first pass the stomach
Correct: the infectious dose can run very high because the vibrios must first pass through the stomach to infect the intestines.
It must first form a spore
Vibrio cholerae forms no spore (an endospore is the Coxiella feature); the dose is high because the vibrios must pass the stomach.

B.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
B.q: Allergic asthma begins with an immediate, IgE-mediated response. When it becomes chronic, the airway inflammation is mediated by T cells, their cytokines and eosinophil granules. Which hypersensitivity type is this chronic phase?
opts: Type IV
Correct: chronic asthma is type IV, delayed and T cell mediated, sustained by cytokines and eosinophil granules; the acute, IgE-mediated phase of allergic asthma is type I.
Type I
Type I, immediate and IgE mediated, is the ACUTE phase of allergic asthma; the chronic phase, mediated by T cells and cytokines, is type IV.
Type II
Type II is free IgG or IgM binding cell surface antigens with complement lysis, as in transfusion reactions, not chronic airway inflammation.
Type III
Type III is immune complexes of IgG or IgM lodging in basement membranes, as in serum sickness, not T cell driven airway inflammation.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, and methods of treatment, and prevention of cocci of medical importance
B.q: What does toxic shock syndrome toxin induce?
opts: Separation of the epidermis
Splitting the upper layers of the epidermis apart is the work of exfoliative toxin rather than toxic shock syndrome toxin.
Lysis of neutrophils
Lysis of neutrophils and macrophages is the work of leukocidin rather than toxic shock syndrome toxin.
Digestion of blood clots
Digesting blood clots is the enzyme staphylokinase rather than toxic shock syndrome toxin.
Fever, vomiting and shock
Correct: the toxin induces fever, vomiting, shock and systemic organ damage, a toxemia that can end in organ failure.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
B.q: Which pair are both drug-resistant forms of Staphylococcus aureus on the superbug list?
opts: Penicillin-sensitive and tetracycline-sensitive
Sensitive strains are not resistant forms; the resistant forms listed are methicillin-resistant and vancomycin-resistant.
Coagulase-negative and catalase-negative
Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase and catalase positive; the resistant forms listed are methicillin-resistant and vancomycin-resistant.
Spore-forming and acid-fast
Staphylococcus aureus is neither spore-forming nor acid-fast; the resistant forms listed are methicillin-resistant and vancomycin-resistant.
Methicillin-resistant and vancomycin-resistant
Correct: the list includes methicillin-resistant (MRSA) and vancomycin-resistant or vancomycin-intermediate Staphylococcus aureus (VRSA, VISA).

B.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire cocci of medical importance
B.q: Which setting raises the risk of meningococcal disease in young adults?
opts: Military field hospitals
Military hospitals are where Acinetobacter baumannii became an important hospital-acquired infection.
College dormitories
Correct: carriage is higher in institutional settings, and those living in close quarters, such as college dorms, are at high risk.
Dental surgery suites
Dental procedures let viridans streptococci into the blood; they are not a named risk for this organism.
Tampon use in women
Tampon use is classically associated with staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
B.q: What shapes can Listeria monocytogenes take?
opts: Coccobacilli to long filaments
Correct: this non-spore-forming Gram-positive ranges from coccobacilli to long filaments, with one to four flagella and no capsule.
Block-shaped rods with spores
Large block-shaped rods with central spores are Bacillus anthracis; Listeria forms no spores.
Branching filaments only
Branching filaments are the shape of Actinomyces and Nocardia rather than Listeria.
Club shapes in palisades
Pleomorphic rods in palisades are Corynebacterium diphtheriae rather than Listeria.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
B.q: Which is the most common form of anthrax?
opts: Pulmonary
Pulmonary anthrax (woolsorters' disease) is the deadliest form rather than the most common one.
Gastrointestinal
Gastrointestinal anthrax follows eating contaminated meat and is far less common than the cutaneous form.
Cutaneous
Correct: cutaneous anthrax, acquired through cuts or incisions in the skin, accounts for the great majority of human cases.
Injection
Injection anthrax has been identified in heroin-injecting addicts in northern Europe and not yet in the United States.

B.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
B.q: What does cromolyn sodium do?
opts: Reduces IgE production by inhibiting lymphocytes
Reducing IgE production by inhibiting lymphocytes is the corticosteroid mechanism.
Blocks degranulation
Correct — it prevents the mast cell from releasing its granule contents rather than blocking the mediators afterwards.
Binds to IgE as a monoclonal antibody
Binding IgE as a monoclonal antibody describes omalizumab rather than cromolyn sodium.
Reverses airway constriction directly
That is epinephrine, which also re-establishes endothelial tight junctions.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, and methods of treatment, and prevention of cocci of medical importance
B.alt: Blood agar plate with two antibiotic discs on the left and, on the right, a pale streak meeting a perpendicular streak with a widened zone where they meet
B.q: A beta-hemolytic streptococcus is streaked toward a streak of Staphylococcus aureus. What does the widened zone where the streaks meet show?
opts: Bacitracin sensitivity
Bacitracin sensitivity is read around a bacitracin disc; a widened zone where two streaks meet is the CAMP reaction.
Partial hemolysis
Partial hemolysis is a greenish zone around colonies, not a widened zone where two streaks meet.
A positive CAMP test
Correct: the CAMP factor works synergistically with beta-hemolytic Staphylococcus aureus to give a flame or arrow shape.
A negative CAMP test
A negative CAMP test shows no enhanced zone where the streaks meet; a widened zone there is a positive result.

B.io: 4 — Describe the mechanism of transfusion reactions
B.q: When does an Rh negative person produce anti-Rh antibodies?
opts: Only after sensitization
Correct — unlike ABO, where antibodies against the antigens you lack are already present, Rh requires prior exposure. A bad transfusion or an incompatible pregnancy does it.
From birth, without any exposure
Rh negative individuals do NOT produce anti-Rh antibodies unless sensitized.
Whenever they encounter any foreign protein
Sensitization is specific, through bad transfusion or incompatible pregnancy.
Only if they are also ABO incompatible
Rh sensitization is independent of ABO grouping and requires prior exposure to Rh positive cells.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
B.q: Which patient fits the high-risk group for which many dentists still give antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work?
opts: A healthy patient having a routine cleaning
Healthy patients do not need prophylaxis; it is limited to high-risk scenarios such as a prosthetic heart valve.
A patient with seasonal allergies
Allergies do not raise the risk dental prophylaxis protects against; a prosthetic heart valve does.
A patient with a prosthetic heart valve
Correct: dental prophylaxis is now limited to a few high-risk scenarios, such as a prosthetic heart valve or a history of endocarditis.
A patient with well-controlled asthma
Asthma is not a high-risk scenario for dental prophylaxis; prosthetic heart valves and prior endocarditis are.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of miscellaneous bacterial agents of human diseases
B.q: Why might erythromycin or tetracycline be used to treat syphilis?
opts: Penicillin is contraindicated
Correct: erythromycin and tetracycline are less effective than penicillin G or doxycycline but can be used when penicillin is contraindicated, for example by patient allergy.
They work better than penicillin
They are LESS effective than penicillin; they are the fallback when penicillin is contraindicated, as in a patient with an allergy.
The disease is tertiary
The stage is not what calls for them; erythromycin and tetracycline are used when penicillin is contraindicated, for example by allergy.
The patient is pregnant
Pregnancy is not the reason given; erythromycin and tetracycline are the fallback when penicillin is contraindicated, for example by allergy.

B.io: 1 — Recall common infectious agents and the diseases that they cause
B.q: Which stains are named for immediate direct examination?
opts: Catalase and oxidase
Catalase and oxidase are biochemical tests performed after growth rather than stains for direct examination.
Bromthymol blue and phenol red
Those are pH indicators used in differential media rather than stains for direct examination.
Gram stain and acid-fast stain
Correct, together with direct fluorescent antibody and direct antigen testing — methods that report before anything has been cultured.
Southern and Northern blots
Southern and Northern blots are electrophoretic techniques for nucleic acids rather than stains.

B.io: 8 — Distinguish between the terms association and causation
B.q: How are most diseases caused?
opts: By an interplay of factors
Correct: a cause is not generally a single factor; most diseases are caused by an interplay of different factors, a web of genes, microbes, environment, behavior and more.
By one necessary factor
A single factor is not the general rule; most diseases arise from an interplay of different factors.
By microbes alone
Microbes are one strand of the web; most diseases are caused by an interplay of factors including genes, environment and behavior.
By genes alone
Genes are one strand of the web of causation; most diseases are caused by an interplay of different factors.

B.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire miscellaneous bacterial agents of human diseases
B.q: What is the reservoir of Chlamydia trachomatis?
opts: Birds
Birds are the source of Chlamydophila psittaci, the cause of ornithosis; Chlamydia trachomatis has a human reservoir.
Rodents
Rodents are reservoirs of Rickettsia typhi and Borrelia hermsii; Chlamydia trachomatis has a human reservoir.
Humans
Correct: Chlamydia trachomatis has a human reservoir; its two strains cause trachoma and lymphogranuloma venereum.
Cattle
Cattle pass Campylobacter fetus between themselves; Chlamydia trachomatis has a human reservoir.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
B.q: An infant who has been fed honey hangs limp, head and limbs drooping, when held face down across an adult's hand, as shown. What syndrome does this illustrate?
B.alt: An infant held face down by an adult.
opts: Neonatal tetanus
Tetanus makes muscles contract uncontrollably, a rigid infant, the opposite of this limp, flaccid one.
Floppy baby syndrome
Correct: a limp infant with flaccid paralysis after honey is floppy baby syndrome, infant botulism, from toxin released after ingested spores germinate.
Neonatal listeriosis
Listeriosis in fetuses and newborns affects the brain and meninges; flaccid paralysis after ingested spores is infant botulism.
Diphtheritic paralysis
Diphtheria is caught by respiratory droplets in non-immunized children and starts with a throat pseudomembrane, not after honey.

B.io: 5 — Define the primary components of public health surveillance
B.q: A prearranged group of providers agrees to report every case of a condition, tracking it for a much larger population. Which type of surveillance is this?
opts: Passive surveillance
Passive surveillance relies on whatever reports facilities submit; a prearranged group agreeing to report all cases is sentinel surveillance.
Sentinel surveillance
Correct: sentinel surveillance uses a prearranged group of reporting sources, usually providers, as a smaller representative group tracking on behalf of a larger population.
Active surveillance
Active surveillance sends staff to contact providers regularly; a prearranged reporting group is sentinel surveillance.
Syndromic surveillance
Syndromic surveillance is defined by case definitions based on clinical features alone; a prearranged representative group is sentinel.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
B.q: Which Gram-positive rod forms a terminal spore that swells one end of the cell?
opts: Bacillus anthracis
Bacillus anthracis is a large, block-shaped rod with a central spore; the terminal spore that swells one end is Clostridium tetani.
Listeria monocytogenes
Listeria monocytogenes is a non-spore-forming regular rod; the rod with a terminal spore swelling one end is Clostridium tetani.
Corynebacterium diphtheriae
Corynebacterium diphtheriae is an irregular, non-spore-forming rod; the terminal spore that swells one end of the rod belongs to Clostridium tetani.
Clostridium tetani
Correct: the Clostridium tetani spore sits at one end of the rod, a terminal spore that swells it; Bacillus anthracis has a central spore instead.

B.io: 1 — Compare and contrast current antibiotic use related to novel antimicrobial therapy
B.q: A critically ill patient with suspected sepsis is started on antibiotics before blood culture results return. What happens to the regimen once results are available?
opts: It is continued unchanged regardless
Empiric therapy is a starting point; it is adjusted once culture and other results are available.
It is always stopped completely
Results may confirm the need for treatment; the regimen is adjusted to them rather than always stopped.
A second empiric drug is always added
Adding drugs automatically is not the rule; the empiric regimen is adjusted to the results.
It is adjusted to fit the results
Correct: empiric therapy is started on experience and antibiograms and then adjusted appropriately, for example in drug choice or by switching intravenous to oral.

B.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
B.q: How is respiratory diphtheria acquired?
opts: Respiratory droplets
Correct: it is acquired via respiratory droplets from healthy carriers or actively infected people.
Contaminated dairy products and deli meat
Dairy and deli meats carry Listeria monocytogenes rather than diphtheria.
Accidental puncture wounds with soil
Puncture wounds with soil introduce Clostridium tetani spores.
Inhaled spores from infected animal wool
Inhaled spores from wool cause pulmonary anthrax; Corynebacterium diphtheriae forms no spores.

C.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of miscellaneous bacterial agents of human diseases
C.q: A false-positive rapid plasma reagin result for syphilis can occur in a patient with which condition?
opts: Cholera
Cholera is not among the conditions that give a false-positive rapid plasma reagin; those listed are human immunodeficiency virus, Lyme disease, some pneumonias, malaria and lupus.
Dental caries
Dental caries is not among the causes of a false-positive rapid plasma reagin; those listed include Lyme disease, malaria and lupus.
Lyme disease
Correct: syphilis tests can give false positives with human immunodeficiency virus infection, Lyme disease, some pneumonias, malaria and lupus.
Trench fever
Trench fever is not among the causes of a false-positive rapid plasma reagin; those listed include Lyme disease, malaria and lupus.

C.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire miscellaneous bacterial agents of human diseases
C.q: How is trench fever spread?
opts: By cat scratches
A cat's clawing injury transmits cat-scratch disease, another Bartonella infection; trench fever is spread by lice.
By tick bites
Ticks spread Lyme disease and Rocky Mountain spotted fever; trench fever is spread by lice.
By inhaled dust
Inhaled particles spread Q fever; trench fever is spread by lice.
By lice
Correct: trench fever, caused by Bartonella, is spread by lice.

C.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-positive bacilli of medical importance
C.q: How does Bacillus cereus most commonly make people ill?
opts: Through deep puncture wounds
Deep puncture wounds are the classic route for Clostridium tetani and for the gas gangrene organisms.
Through contaminated food
Correct: it is most commonly a foodborne illness; its spores are very commonly airborne and dustborne and land on foods.
Through respiratory droplets
Respiratory droplets spread Corynebacterium diphtheriae and Mycobacterium tuberculosis rather than Bacillus cereus.
Through contact with armadillos
Armadillos are a possible zoonotic source of leprosy, not of Bacillus cereus.

C.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, and methods of treatment, and prevention of cocci of medical importance
C.q: Which staphylococcal lesion is a boil, in which a hair follicle or sebaceous gland progresses into an abscess?
opts: Carbuncle
A carbuncle is the larger, deeper lesion formed when a cluster of furuncles aggregates and interconnects.
Folliculitis
Folliculitis is superficial inflammation of the hair follicle that usually resolves; it can progress to a furuncle.
Impetigo
Impetigo is bubble-like swellings that break and peel away rather than a single follicular abscess.
Furuncle
Correct: a furuncle is a boil, inflammation of a hair follicle or sebaceous gland that progresses into an abscess or pustule.

C.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, and methods of treatment, and prevention of cocci of medical importance
C.alt: Blood agar plate with bacterial colonies, a second example
C.q: What does the change in the medium around and beneath these colonies show, where the red blood agar has turned greenish?
opts: Complete (beta) hemolysis
Complete, beta, hemolysis leaves a clear zone around the colonies rather than a greenish one.
No hemolysis at all
With no hemolysis the red medium would look unchanged; a greenish change around the colonies is partial hemolysis.
A positive CAMP test
A positive CAMP test is a flame or arrow shape where a streak meets a Staphylococcus aureus streak, not a greenish zone.
Partial (alpha) hemolysis
Correct: partial, alpha, hemolysis gives the greenish color, the reaction of Streptococcus pneumoniae and the viridans group.

C.io: 2 — Compare and contrast the types of hypersensitivities and diseases caused by hypersensitivity conditions
C.q: What do basophils initiate?
opts: A TH2 response and production of IgE
Correct. They are rare granulocytes, and in normal defense they act against helminths — the same axis that produces allergy when misdirected.
A TH1 response and production of IgG
The response they initiate is TH2 with IgE, which is the allergic axis.
Complement activation by the classical pathway
Complement activation characterizes types II and III rather than the basophil's initiating role.
Cytotoxic T cell proliferation
Cytotoxic T cells belong to type IV responses rather than to the basophil-driven IgE axis.

C.io: 9 — Define the terms endemic, epidemic, pandemic, sporadic, and herd immunity
C.alt: A bar chart of diarrheal illness in city residents by date of onset from mid-December to mid-January, bloody and nonbloody cases stacked; arrows mark water main breaks in late December, a boil-water order in early January and chlorination later; cases rise over about two weeks and fall away after the boil-water order.

C.q: This epidemic curve follows diarrheal illness in city residents for several weeks after water main breaks, falling away after a boil-water order. Which type of epidemic does it show?
opts: Common source, continuous
Correct: the residents shared one source, the water supply, over a longer time than one incubation period, so cases kept coming until the source was dealt with: a continuous common source.
Common source, point
A point source is a brief exposure within one incubation period, giving one sharp peak; weeks of exposure to the water supply make it continuous.
Propagated
Propagated spread is person to person in successive waves; cases tied to the water supply over weeks are a continuous common source.
Sporadic
Sporadic describes isolated incidents at irregular intervals, not an epidemic curve of many linked cases; this is a continuous common source.

The endospore

The inclusion body

C-carbohydrate

Fimbriae

Streptolysin S

C.io: 3 — Describe the primary methods of diagnosing, treating, and preventing allergies
C.q: What does prevention of allergy involve?
opts: Taking antihistamines daily regardless of exposure
Antihistamines bind histamine receptors on target organs; that is pharmacological control, not prevention.
Injecting small amounts of the allergen
Injecting small amounts of allergen is desensitization, the third management approach, not prevention.
Administering epinephrine prophylactically
Epinephrine reverses airway constriction in a reaction; prevention avoids exposure to the allergen in the first place.
Modifying environment and behavior
Correct: prevention means modifying the environment and behaviors so as to avoid exposure to the allergen.

C.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, and methods of treatment, and prevention of cocci of medical importance
C.q: Which Staphylococcus aureus toxin lyses neutrophils and macrophages?
opts: Enterotoxin
Enterotoxin induces gastrointestinal distress and causes staphylococcal food intoxication.
Exfoliative toxin
Exfoliative toxin splits the upper layers of the epidermis apart, producing scalded skin syndrome.
Leukocidin
Correct: leukocidin lyses leukocytes, especially neutrophils and macrophages, the cells sent to attack the organism.
Coagulase
Coagulase is an enzyme that coagulates plasma and blood rather than a toxin that lyses white cells.

C.io: 1 — Recall common infectious agents and the diseases that they cause
C.q: What do physiological and biochemical characteristics detect?
opts: The chemical composition of the cell wall
That is chemical analysis, which examines cell wall peptides and membrane lipids.
The presence or absence of enzymes
Correct, read as physiological reactions to nutrients. Catalase, oxidase, coagulase and the hemolysins are among the common tests. Metabolic pathways are read the same way.
Colony pigment and texture
Colony pigment and texture are macroscopic morphological features read from the plate.
The sequence of the 16S ribosomal RNA gene
Sequencing the 16S ribosomal RNA gene is a genotypic method used to construct phylogenies.

C.io: 7 — Describe selected measures of morbidity and mortality
C.q: As testing of mild cases expands during an outbreak, what tends to happen to the case fatality rate?
opts: It is overestimated
Overestimation is the early problem, when the sickest cases are the ones hospitalized and counted; wider testing of mild cases pushes the estimate down.
It is underestimated

Correct: the case fatality rate may be overestimated at first, when the sickest cases are hospitalized, and then underestimated as testing of mild cases increases; a long time to resolution can also make it look better than it is.
It becomes exact
More testing does not make it exact; adding many mild cases to the denominator tends to underestimate it.
It is no longer defined
It is still deaths over total cases; adding mild cases to the denominator tends to make it an underestimate.

C.io: 7 — Differentiate between primary and secondary immunodeficiency conditions
C.q: A young boy has recurrent bacterial infections and no detectable antibodies. Which defect is most likely?
opts: A B cell defect
Correct. Agammaglobulinemia is a B cell defect; the patient lacks antibodies and suffers more bacterial infections.
A T cell defect
T cell defects such as DiGeorge syndrome bring recurrent fungal, protozoan, helminth and viral infections instead.
An acquired viral infection
A virus such as the human immunodeficiency virus causes SECONDARY immunodeficiency by targeting T helper cells, not congenital absence of antibody.
A mast cell defect
Mast cells mediate allergy; recurrent bacterial infection with no antibody points to B cells.

C.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, and methods of treatment, and prevention of cocci of medical importance
C.q: Why do staphylococci stain Gram-positive?
opts: A thin peptidoglycan layer
A thin peptidoglycan layer is the envelope of the Gram-negative cocci such as Neisseria, which stain Gram-negative.
A protective outer capsule
Staphylococci MAY produce a capsule, a protective layer exterior to the cell wall, but the Gram-positive reaction comes from the thick peptidoglycan.
A thick peptidoglycan layer
Correct: staphylococci stain Gram-positive because of the thick peptidoglycan in their cell envelope, which also makes Gram-positive cells physically strong.
A layer of internal spores
Staphylococci lack spores, so spores cannot explain the stain; the Gram-positive reaction comes from the thick peptidoglycan.

Stool banks of screened donor samples
Correct: there are stool banks to make this therapeutic option more accessible, holding screened donor stool samples.
Synthetic stool made in factories
The material is not synthetic: it is screened donor stool, collected and held in stool banks.
Antibiotic-treated stool
Stool is not treated with antibiotics; stool banks of screened donor samples make it accessible.

C.q: What is familial about allergy?
opts: The specific allergen a person reacts to
The inherited element is the general predisposition rather than the specific allergy.
The route by which allergens enter
Portal of entry is determined by exposure rather than inherited.
A generalized predisposition
Correct — families inherit the tendency rather than the particular allergen, which is why relatives may react to entirely different things. The specific allergy is not inherited.
Nothing — allergy has no familial component
A generalized predisposition to allergies is specifically described as familial.
